result:
There is something quietly moving about finding pencil marks in a used book—a stranger's underline beneath a sentence you happened to love too, a small "ha!" scribbled beside a joke, a question mark hovering next to a passage that confused someone decades ago. It's a form of conversation across time, one participant absent, both readers bent over the same page like two people leaning over the same well.

I think about how much of human thought has traveled this way—not through grand declarations but through marginal traces. The notes in monastery manuscripts where a tired scribe complained about cold hands. The letters between friends who argued about poetry and accidentally invented new ways of seeing. History feels monumental from a distance, but up close it's mostly people muttering to themselves in the margins of bigger texts.

Maybe that's why I find the internet both magnificent and melancholy. We've built the largest margin ever—billions of comments, replies, reactions layered over everything—and yet so little of it will survive the way a pencil mark survives. Paper forgives neglect; servers do not. A library can burn once and still leave fragments. A hard drive fails silently and leaves nothing at all.

Perhaps the lesson is to annotate boldly anyway. Underline what moves you. Argue with authors who can't answer back. Write "how lovely" in the margins of your own life, even if no one reads it later. The trace matters less for whoever finds it than for the hand that made it—the act of noticing, made visible, however briefly, before the page closes again.
